Foreign Intelligence. þÿ In the urgent pressure of the concerns of our country, the current routine business of our foreign neighboms necessarily sinks into comparative insignificance In France, they are suffering much under the same distress as in England, bui the French government, still retaining all its usual military still and commissariat, and much of the habiis of the people to submit to this military organ sation to a greater extent than would be practicable in England, has been enabled to take more effectual measures to niford temporary relief, and to carry it at once into the places which most exigently require it. Their whole system of relief is conducted on the commissariat plan and by commissariat officers. These are sent into the towns and districts which suller most þÿ They buy and collect food at the nearest poits, and thence transmit it to the remote towns where it is sold at something less than cost price, and thus distributed as far as it can go. In Portugal, the civil war is nearly at an end, though Oporto still holds out. In Spam, affairs aie slil! very unsettled, lion Enrique had been suddenly ordered away from Madrid to Barcelona, on i t»e discovery of his intended marriage wilh a lady of the Court; the lady . herself has been sent to a convent. The daughter of Hon Francisco de Paula was married a few days since to theGount H'Aliamira. Revolutionary svmptoms are again manifesting themselves in Catalonia and oilier provinces. gence from America, except that the Mexican war is to be vigorously continued, and
that the Congress have rejected a lesolution pioposed by the moderate party, that the object of the war is not conquest and annexation. So much for the moderation of a Republican government.

Professor von Grusselhach of Stockholm, has very lately brought to a state of pei lection the art of producing a torpor of die whole system, by the application of cold of different degrees of intensity, producing from a lesser to n greater, so as to cause the human body to become torpid without permanent injury to any organ or tissue ol t lie frame. In this slate they may remain a great number ol yearn, and again, alter a sleep of ages, be awakened to existence, as fresh and blooming as thev were when they first sunk into their frigoric slumber. The attention of the learned professor was first led to the subject by finding a toad enclosed in a solid fiagnient of calcareous rock 10 lent in diameter, which when taken out, showed unequivocal signs of life; but it was supposed that the concussion r eused by blasting the rock occasioned his death in a

few hours after The opinion of Raion Gruithizen, who is geologist to the King ol Sweden, was, that it must have been in that situation for at least 7000 years; and his calculations were drawn from the different lavers of strata by which it w as surrounded. From this hint, the professor proceeded to make experiments ; and after a laborious course of experiments for the last 29 years of his life, he has at last succeeded in perfecting this great discovery No less than fit), 000 reptiles, shell lish, &e. were experimented on before he tiied the human subject. One was a Swedish girl, aged, from appearance, about 19 years ; was consigned to the professor by order of the Government to experiment upon, having been found guilty of murdering her child. With the exception of a slight paleness, she appeared as if asleep, although she has been in a state of complete torpor, for 1wo years lie intends, be savs. to resuscitate her in five more years, and convince the world of the soundness of bis wonderful discovery. 1 be professor, to gratify us. took a small snake out of his cabinet into another room, and although it appeared to us to lie perfectly dead and rigid as marble, by application of a mixture of cayenne pepper and brandy, it showed immediate signs of life, and was apparently as active as ever it was in a few minutes,

From the St Thomas Times. March 20. THE TWEED. We are enabled through the courtesy of It. HL l,m;su Esq., the superintendent of the It. M. S. Company, in this island, to furnish our readers with the following particulars which may be relied on for accuracy relative to the loss of the above noble steamer. On the 12th of February, whilst on her wav to Vera Cruz from Havana, and not vice versa, as we erroneously staled in our supplement of yestetdav ; she struck on the Alacrnne Reef, at 3" 30" a. m. audio 30 minutes went to pieces. Captain Pars' ns who was on the upper deck at the time, was washed ovoiboard, but providentially reached the teef in safety. The whole of theupier portion of the niter part of the as vessel washed awav instantaneously she struck, was and was seen no more, causing so deplorable and such large ioss of life among the passengers- The accident is supposed to have been occasioned by a strong current setting to the north, occasioned hv the long prevalence of northerly winds along the Mexican þÿcoast. Among those who perished were five ladies, Mr Cooke the 4ih officer and Messrs. Spence and Varlal midshipmen Every boat was lost hut one, which was found stove in on the reef. She was patched up in the best manner that could lie done under such circumstances l.i'-uteiianl Davns R. N. with Mr. El win the chief oflicer, proceeded in her io Sisal, where they aimed in safety, and found a small Spanish brig which sailed immediately and took the survivors off the reef where they had been on a rail which they

had managed to construct, for five riavs and nights without either food or water, sufleiing agonies of mind and body which can be better imagined than described. The conduct of the Commander of the Spanish brig was noble in the extreme, and we regret that al present we are ignoiant of his name t mt we might record it in due terms, and pay him the tribute he so justly deserves, for lie remained on shore on the reel through the night with the shipwrecked sutFerers striving by every means to cheer them, and impart confidence and hope that on the following morn they would be released from their perilous and dreadful situation. We are authorized to state for public information that arrangements have been made by the proper authorities which will prevent anv poilion of the mail service being deranged in consequence of this lamentable cnsuality. The correspondent of a French paper writes from Constantinople on the 20th ult: þÿ Tite Sultan yesterday presided at a sitting of the Supreme Council of Justice, all the ministers and high functionaries being present. þÿI he Sultan himself proposed a measure which will produce a great sensation in Europe, namely, to issue an ordonnance for the suppression of lire slave market. This is not indeed a suppression ul slavery altogether hut it is a first step towards it. The Koran, it is true, admits of slavery, but it is only in tolerance, for it at the same time recommends the enfranchisement of slaves as a meritorioh action; and the rich Musselmans, at their great family festivals, or before setting out on a long journey, and indeed at an important event of their lives, helie'e they cannot do anything more agreeable to God Ilian to give a slave his freedom. The obstacles to general emancipation arise rather from the customs and manners of the Turks than from religious prejudices ; and from the moment the Sultan sets the example, it w ill meet with ready imitation. 'Ihe Bey of Tunis has already abolished slavery in his Regency, and Ibrahim þÿl acha, on his return from Europe, gave freedom to all his slaves, without either of these acts producing the least mark of disapprobation in the Musselmaa states. All the world knows that in these states the slaves lor in a part of the family to which they belong, and that many reach important stations. Two of the present

ministers of the Sultan, Kosrew þÿl acha, and Haliz þÿl acha, are freed slaves, so were the late Governor of Trebisond, son in law of Sultan Mahmoud, Halil þÿI aclia, Muliemet lleschid þÿl acha, commander in chief of Hie army of Arabia, and many olheis. Tie mother of Ihe Sultan mid all his wives were Circassian or Georgian slaves who have been enfranchised. The whole question turns on tliis point, that no man can hold a tight over the ftecdom of a fellow creature."

(From the Bury Herald ) On Monday last a large assemblage of the professional gentlemen of this vto.m ty took place at the Suffolk General Hospital, to witness the operation of removing a tumour from the breast of a female, while under the influence of the vapour ol ether. Some difficulty was expeiienced in bringing the patient fully under the influence of the ether j but this was at length effected, and she was laid back on the pillows in a state of complete insensibility. 'The operation was then commenced, and the tumour, about the size of an orange, was raptbly removed by Air. Image, the patient making only an indistinct moaning noise. As some dissection was necessary in order to separate th ; diseased part, the woman had a second application of the inhaler, so that the insensibility was maintained as long as was required. And now came the most interesnng part ol the procedure. A towel having I een laid over the bosom, so as to conceal the effects of the operation, and the patient having recovered her senses, Dr. Hanking asked her how she felt, and whether she was now read to undergo the operation ? Site replied that she was quite resigned and willing: that she knew that it must be painful, but that Mr Image might commence as soon as he liked. This answer was elicited from her several times by Dr, Hanking, that the spectators might have a full opportunity of ascertaining that she was perfectly unaware of any operation having been performed. Dr. Hanking then informed her that the tumour hud aliea-

dv been removed, and that nothing mote was to be done, upon which her countenance put on an expression of delighted and grateful astonishment which it is impossible to depict. In fact, she appeared quite incredulous, until she had raised her head, and hersell inspected the wound, when she could not sufficiently thank those around her for having been spared an amount of suffering which s ie had justly supposed would, under ordinary circumstances, have been extreme. Nothing could, in the estimation of the majority present, have been more demonstrative of the power ol this agent than the pieserit case. It was one which required careful dissection, and was not, therefore, so rapid as others. 'The expression of willingness to submit to the supposed impending operation was genuine, as were also the incredulity and subsequent gratitude. 'The woman has since positively declared, that ' she felt nothing, but was in a dream, and taken away from the present world-" Her pulse and general aspect were not like those of a pierson who had so large a poition of the body excised. M'he application was tried last week by Mr. Smith, a< ibe hospital, in a severe case of cancer on the lip, but the symptoms <f congestion of the brain were so apparent, that be thought it more prudent to delay the operation. Several successful cases of extraction of teeth have been performed at the same institution, under the influence ol tie vapour ; and it has been repeatedly (tied Upton a medical student, for the purpose of
showing the insensibility to prain which it piroiiuc.es. and the geueral barmlessncss of its operation.

The authorities of Canada are engaged in driving, from their homes, at the present inclement season of the year, nearly one hundred families, containing about eleveu hundred persons, who have sealed and made improvements upon a tract of land lying upon the Grand River. The lands in question were surrendered to the Crown by the Indians, ami afterwards appropriated to the Five Nations, who were dispossessed of their lands in the United States during the Revolutionary war. In 1841 they were again surrendered, excepting a parcel known as Johnson's tract. There is no right of preemption to this land, but the settlers claim it according to the former usage and practice of the Government, and in default of any notice that it was excepted from the pre eruption right. The Toronto Examiner comments with severity upon the course pursued by the government, in driving these people off. without the means of sheltering themselves, in the midst of a Canadian w inter. þÿ lfi.fl Adv.

LATER FROM THE BRAZOS. The schooner Lone Star, Captain Minor, arrived on the 2d instant, bom ll»e mouth of the Kio Grande, having sailed on the 25 b, one day alter the Telegraph. The I'.oayune of the 3rd instant has no letters by litis irr i v at. but are indebted to Capl Minor lot a copy of the Matamoras Hug ot the 2.1 Quite the most interesting matter contained in the Flag are two letters from .Santa Anna, translated by the Flag (with oilier letters we have before seen) fiom papeis ot Vn: ori t de Tanau'ipas We lay them at once before our readers. They show how complete was the discomfiture of Sama Anna, and how terrible his losses. He repeats ihe old siory notoriously untrue, that we had I), ODD men and 20 pieces of artillery iu the action. To Hen. Don Circiaco Vasque z. Agua Nuev.a, Feb. 25, 1847. My Esteemed, þÿtriend The hasie with which 1 sent off the last express to the Government hindered me from writing to you ihe news of the deeds of arms. We have f«>u»ht for two whole days. The enemy awaited us at a point called the Narrows. The battle of the 23rd was particularly bloody on both sides but it was impossible to take the principal position ot the enemy, which is another Thermopylae, although we drove him f'om five positions and took two banners and three guns. The blood run in torrents, and it is calculated that both armies lost three or lour thousand men in killed and wounded. Our bayonet charges resulted in the death of hundreds but the enemy could not be completely routed on account of the strong position ha

occupied We gave him to understand that the Mexican soldier can fight bravely, breast to breast, and without being deterred either by strength of position, nor by brokenness of ground, nor by hunger and thirst, which he sutfeied with heroic resignation. The strength of the enemy was 9,000 men and 26 pieces of artillery. IV e have to lament the death ot Col. Berra, Lieut. Col. Amnios, and the commanders of battalion and squadrons. I.uyando, Kio lVnn, besides other officers. Gen. Lombardino, Col. IJi iio. Col Kocha, Gen. Angel Guzman, Lieut. Cols. Gallozo, Monterdeoca, Andrade, Jicoleical Ouijano, Basave, Onate, and other chiefs and officers are wounded. I lost mv horse by a gun shot in one of the first charges. We ore destitute of necesssarics for the wounded, and 1 therefore charge vou to send on immediately the provisions in your place, s<> that they may meet the army, which has done its duty nnd saved the honor of the national arms. God and Liberty ! Santa Anna.

To his Excellency I). Ramon Adame. Agfa Nuf.va Feb 26, 1847. My Dear þÿFriend The burrv in which I wrote my last letter prevented me from sending you a copy of my despatch to the G»veminent and (he general order issued to the troops on the field of ba'Hc, I now send it. and suppose the triumph of our arms has been

celebrated iti your town. The warn of sop plies together wiih the djsenlciy, which broke out in the anny, compelled me to listen to the opinions of tlte general and chiefs of the army, and regulate my operations accordingly, They unanimously determined that the army ought to fall back on points where supplies might be tiad. I have therefore determined to retire by way of Oedral, Vanegas and Matehulae, where I can establish a hospital for the wounded, who amount to more than 400. and also for tfie sick ; after which 1 will return and seek the enemy, pro. vided the Government furnishes the necessary resources. 1 have informed the government to this effect under the present date. 1 here take occasion to state, as all the world should know it, that the treason of a native Mexican prevented me from gaining a complete victo ry over our invaders. A soldier from the regiment of curassiers, a native of Saltillo, deserted from Encarnacion and informed Gen. Wool of my approach. Gen. Wool precipitately struck Ins camp, abandoning a part of his train and some provisions, and occupied the impregnable position nt Angostura, which it was impossile to reduce, not withstanding the great advantage gamed by our troops; who took live of their positions, three stands of colors and as many pieces of artillery. God and Liberty ! Santa Anna.

þÿ þÿ>otvn« Gen. Taylor's Address to the Army. The Union, in publishing the subjoined "Older" issued by Gen. Taylor after the battle of Buena Vista remarks; It is written in fine taste. It alludes in the most modest terms which he could employ to the brilliant victory which our troops have won over the immense superiority ol the Mexicans headed by their most distinguished military leader. It pnvs due honors to the brave troops and officers who live to receive the gratitude of their country. It pays a brief furl affecting tribute to those gallant spirits who have gloriously fallen in battle, but whose "illustrious" example will remain for the benefit and admiration of tlte army, and as a monument cf ihe glory of our republic in the eyes of Europe. It treats as delicately as possible nil those inexperienced soldiers who ingloriouslv lied to whom he administers the warning lesson of seeking to recover their reputation by future exertion on another field. It is impossible to read the various descriptions of this memorable battle, where the skill of the commanding general in seizing his ground and maneuvering his troops vied with the chivalry of his men without the deepest emotion.

A large number of bystanders sided with the carman, abused Mademoiselle Lola, and grew so exasperated, that, deemed tier position a peiilous one, she threw herself into a chemists'. shop and shot the door so violent!) that a number of panes >f glass were shattered. She teplied twenty eight years. DiscovEKY op a Singular Race of People- þÿ 1 lie C aicutla Christian Observer lor January gives notice of a singular race of a people called the Kailnes, who inhabit a part o( Guzerat : þÿ " These people are supposed by some to be the ancient Cathie, who in the time of Alexander's invasion occupied a poitiou of the Punjuub, near the confluence of 1 lie five riveis. Among the Ratines there aie no distinctions of casts. Besides priests, they have an official class of persons called bards, who possess authority almost equal 10 that of the Druids. They become security for the payment of debts, the conduct of individuals who have misbehaved, and the appearance of persons in pending actions, either civil or criminal. On the same terms they conduct travellers and caravans through districts invested with robbers, or in a state of war. If a troop of predatory horse appear, the bard commands them to retire; and, brandishing his dagger, takes a solemn oath, that if they plunder the persons under his protection, he w ill stab himself to the heart, and bring upon their heads the guilt of shedding his blood. fSuch is the veneration in which he is held as n person of celestial origin, and such is the horror at being the cause of his death, that the threat in almost every instance deteis them from making the meditated attack, and the party is allowed to pass on unmolested. The religion of these people consists of little else than adoration of the sun.

They invoke this object of their worship before commencing any great ondei taking, and if a plundering expedition lie successful, a portion of the money stolen is consecrated to the service of religion. The only functions of the priests are to celebrate marriages and funeral solemnities. They have but one sacred building, a temple, situated near Thuam, dedicated to the sun, and containing an image of that luminary. The size of the Kalhies is above the average, often exceeding six feet. The women aie tall and often handsome: generally speaking, modest, and faithful to their lords. The Kalhies have 110 restrictions of any sort regarding food or diitik "

Great Revolution in Steam PRO- PULSION. This heading will startle many of our readers Ingenuity lias been exhausted in devising an improvement on the piesent mode ot propelling ships by steam. Against the old paddle wheels strong objections as to the loss of power, and oilier draw hacks upon a sleamei þÿ s progress have been urged, winch it would he useless to lepeal lieie, lor they are well known to practical engineers and seamen ; and a remedy was sought lor in the smew. This screw has been only partially successful, as its limited adaptation proves. The only vessel ot note to w hich it has been applied is the Great Britain, and the unfortunate teiminntion ol her career hardly gave the new invention a lair trial on a large scale. But a discovery has now been pet lected by Mr. IS. 11 þÿI aikhutst. a gentleman ot great mechanical ingenuity, which most supersede the existing modes ol steam propulsion, and revolutionise the tralltc i>v sea This invention is secured by patent in Great Britain and all Iter colonies, the United Slates. France, and all other parts ol the world. It is not merely original, but, like most useful inventions, remarkably, nay, beautifully simple The advantages are threefold a greatly increased rate ol speed, a vastly increased power of stowage, hv the reduction of the present cumbrous machinery in the holds of steamers. It is difficult to make out selves clear on these points without the aid of a diagram. But we may state, briefly, that a number of submerged vertical propel-

lers are to he fixed on each side of the vessel ; these revolve in unison, and by the force with which they take hold of the water, and the power which this combined action gives then', send forward the ship at a speed aliooeilit-r unattainable by the present or any kimwir system. It has been asserted, bv practical men, that a vessel so propelled would cross the Atlantic in nearly half the time of the best steamers now employed in ocean navigation. Some eminent engineers, who admitted that the theory ot the new plan was excellent, doubted its practicability A model which was exhibited some lime ago. and received th«- encomiums ol the Lords of the Admiralty, showed the principle clearly, but doubts legitimate doubts at ihe þÿlime were thrown

on its adaptation. The experiments this week, by the application of sientn to the new discovery, have settled the question ol its success. During the last week the steamengine has propelled these new vertical paddies which are made of iron, at the raie of 23 miles an hour, and has removed all doubts on the minds of those who were previously the most sceptical. We cannot dilate on the importance ot this greatest ol modern inventions with regard to steam navigation; but this vve may say, that since the day s of Arkwright nothing equal in importance to it has appeared, and we expect it will remain a brilliant proof of the genius and the judgment of the inventor. þÿ Wi liner and þÿSmith sLuropean Tunes.

Feeling rather fatigued liom a long walk, and liom seeing the operations, 1 determined to refiesh myself by a few inhalations of the ether 1 shall never forget the extraordinary ellects which were produced upon me. At the first trial i made six or eight inspirations; during the first two or thtee the taste of ether was rather unpleasant, and produced a slight irritation, but that passed away, and I fell very much refreshed and elevated in spirits, and altogether very comfortable. At the end of eight or nine inspirations 1 left off; I then had a feeling pretty much analogous to that which is experienced alter the third or fourth glass of good port wine. 1 was somewhat elevated, with a slight connection across the forehead and a disposition to be cheerful and talkative. After a minute or so I applied the mouthpiece again, the vapour had more relish; I drank, as it were, more deeply, and found my arms begin to move against my will, I breathed still more deeply and more quickly, and found that my appetite was insatiable. 1 could not drain it enough, and became violently excited, and I fell the instrument taken from me by force. Alter it was removed from my mouth, I seemed to be exaspetaled and to breath more forcibly than ever, and as much pleased and refreshed with the coolness of the air, and i know I made a great noise while expiring and inspiring. My muscular exertions now got entirely beyond my control, ) knew where 1 was. I knew what 1 had been doing,

that some gentlemen weie attempting to hold me, but 1 did not feel their gtipes, 1 cared for nobody or nothing. It was the only time in tnv life that I could have gone through fire and water ior the mere fun of the thing. 1 should have liked to have smashed every thing that came in my way, and I lelt it was foolish for the gentlemen to try to hold me 1 fell a very Sampson þÿ and wondered I did not see llioge attempting to hold me stietched upon the floor, i could not see why they wished to hold me, and could not account for my position. My ideas were very indistinct, rapid, and changefol, and 1 seemed to have no definite object in view, but merely a deteimination not to be restrained from doing what 1 wished to do, and yet i do not know what that was. At this moment, 1 seemed to have lost myself for a twinkling þÿ I felt myself falling apparently though myself come down a considerable on the floor depth, and felt with a tr< mendous crash ; yet without the slightest pain. My consciousness now returned to me. 1 fell the extraordinary state in which 1 was þÿ sill muscular power gone þÿ 1 lay immoveable ; and yet could see and hear eieiy thing that was said. Being alarmed, and apprehending i was dying, and that i could do nolhi' g for myself, 1 instantly said, þÿ Gentlemen, although 1 am incapable of moving. see you ail, and hear every word you say " My feelings at this moment were most extraordinary þÿ in fact, awful, I did not know whether my voice was articulate, and that 1 could Ire

comprehended. I ueaid you sav, þÿ Just as I thought ; 1 told you how it would be. Upon hearing this 1 became more alarmed ; my moments seemed numbered; all my past sins passed before my mind's c\e ; I thought of my friends, and all that 1 loved; 1 hit I never should see them iitorc. 1 would have given all 1 possessed for a chance of life;

-- þÿ--and seeing myself surrounded by medical men, 1 said in a solemn and serious manner, i call upon you as medical men lo consult together, without loss ot lime, and see what is to he done, for 1 am a dead man." When I had delivered my speech ) saw one of you smile. 1 said, þÿ may li be laughing to you, but to me it is a serious þÿmailer. You now tol l me that 1 should soon recover, and dial it was all rigid. A correspondent of the New York Tribune giving a desciiptiou of British railways, says : þÿ " 1'he English railways are admirable. 1 happened to take the express train, and we made 50 miles tire hour easy. You will find no corduroy post roads here as in Georgia or Alabama, nor lines of rail over which milk may be churned to butter every five miles. Indeed i tie roads ought to he good þÿ a country small in exient thickly, ay. densely populated, with a thousand years of age and enormous wealth, besides being continually well taxed, should present some perfection in load making more than could be expected from a partial wilderness 30 times its size, and as yet hardly drained of a morass. The length of rail between New York and Philadelphia, for example, laid down anvwheie in England, would intersect 10 times the population. This alone were a strong reason for better roads than ours, for the travel affords it. But our faults in the railway system result more from the immature soil, 1 reckon, than a want of capital. They are capitally bridged where a crossing is ncces-ary, protected with walls or fences along the line, besides having policemen stationed within sight of each oiher the whole length of the road. wiies are constructed upon most of the roads and the departure of each train is announced from station to station to doubly avoid collisions. The station houses and depots arc fine þÿ no smoking allowed in or about lliem or the cars, and they are not, as with us, victualling shops."

From the Rochester Daily Aim tiser. As IsTEtlBSTING SCENE. þÿ A SCCtlC of touching interest occurred in the Executive chamber, at Albany, a few days since. A year or more ago, our readers may recollect, a Methodist minister, of ptevious good character, was convicted in one of ihe La»tcin counties of the crime of forgery, and sentenced to the state prison for a term of seats. þÿ Since It is incarceration, an effort had been made on the part of his friends to get hitn pardoned, but without success, and the pioject was abandoned. Not so wi i h his daughter, an interesting girl of some eighteen or twenty years. Site thought if she could only see the Governor, the eloquence of her tears, and the truthfulness of her story would produce the desued result. Aided by a few friends she journeyed to Albany, determined not to return until she could carry to her mother the pardon (or her father. She called upon the Executive, and in a simple and unpretending manner related her grievances, and pleaded with the eloquence of a loving heart, for the liberation of her parent, who, although disgraced, uas her parent still. Every day, loo. we conversed of God. of the soul, its capacity to enjoy and sutler in this life and the next, and there was pleasure in seeing that his mind was ripening rapidly, and his thoughts fastening on heavenly and divine things. When 1 left the Seminary 1 took leave of him, hut have never ceased to feel a lively interest in his situation. His subsequent his torv is worthy of being recorded for the physician and the Christian, and 1 find a melan cltoly satisfaction in gathering the following facts. Ilis father removed with him to this city, where he died on the 9th ult , aged 126 years. He was the brother of the Rev. J. A- Cary, professor in the Deaf and Dumb Asylum here. For neatly twenty years Charles Augustus Cary had been the victim of a disease of a scrofulous rheumatic character, which was at times exceedingly painful. In its progress everv joint in his svstem became stiffened, so that he was deprived entirely of the use of his limbs and became incapable of voluntary motion, except in the muscles attached to the face. His mental powers were naturally of a high order, and his bodily infirmities exerted onlv in no indirect way an unfavorable influence on their development. He had nearly completed the studies preparatory to a col I giate course of education, when the disease reached, almost simultaneously, his hands and eyes, and deprived him, ever after, of their assistance in his personal efforts for mental improvement. Tub Rural Population of China. The farms ate small, each consisting of from one to four or five acres ; indeed, every cottager has his own little tea garden, the produce of which supplies the wauls of his family, and the surplus firings him in a few dollars, which are spent on the other necessaries of life. The same system is practised in everything relating to Chinese agriculture. The cotton, silk, and rice farms, are generally all small, and managed upon the same plan. There are few sights more pleasing than a Chinese family in the interior engaged in gathering the tea leaves, or, indeed, in any of their other agricultural pursuits. There is the old man. it may lie the grandfather, or even t fie great grandfather, patiiatch like, directing Ins descendants, many of whom are in their youth amt prime, while others ate in theii childhood, in (tie labours of the field He stands in the turds' of them, bowed down with age. Rut, to the honour of the Chinese as a lint toil, he is always looked up to bv all with pride and affection, and Ins old age and grey hairs aie honoured, revered, and loved. When, after the labours of the day are over they return to their humble and happy homes, their fare consists chiefly of rice, fish, and vegetables, which they enjoy with great zt st, and are happy and contented, 1 really believe that there is no country in the woild where the agricultural population are better off than they ate in the north of China. Labour with them is pleasure, for its fruits
are eaten by themselves, and the rod of the oppressor is unfell and unknown. þÿ Foilune's W anUriings in China.

Wonders of the Electric Telegraph. þÿ An experiment, completely successful, was witnessed some time since, in the Isle of Wight, of the powers of Mr. Mott's electric telegraph. A perfect nnd rapid communication was established between East and West Cowes by means of a single wire sunk act oss t he channel. The telegraphs were attached, one being placed at the Medina Hotel, and the other at the opposite side of the charnel, near the Fountain Hotel. The signal hells were then rung simultaneously. and the telegraphs commenced working and communicating questions and answers with the greatest precision and certainty with a galvanic battery of low power, showing that a single isolated wire immersed in the water could carry the electiic current a distance of half a mile. The water brought hack the current to its source without the slightest perceptible dispersion or loss of the dynamic power. This experiment demnnstiates the perfect practicability of submarine communication, and the question as to its application may he said to he satisfactorily solved. The cons quences can scarcely be as yet appreciated, though they are wonderful to contemplate.
